title: Adaptive kernel orchestration and KV-cache profiling notes
body:
Purpose
---
Notes from exploratory experiments combining Triton, TensorRT and our in-house custom kernels with an emphasis on: kernel orchestration, fallback behavior, and KV-cache memory/layout compatibility. This is intended to capture what we tried, early profiling numbers, key tradeoffs, and next experiments to converge on an operational design for multi-kernel serving.

Background and motivations
---
- We need runtime-level flexibility to pick the best kernel backend per model+workload (latency-sensitive vs throughput).
- Triton gives us orchestration and multi-backend management; TensorRT gives high single-model perf for NVIDIA GPUs; custom kernels (our CUDA/metal fused attention work) provide lower memory footprint and specialized quantized paths.
- Challenge: KV-cache layout differences and quantization mean a model served by one kernel is not necessarily compatible with state created by another. Customers expect graceful fallbacks and canary rollouts, so we need a coherent strategy.

Goals for this doc
---
- Record experiments and profiling to inform a design for: (a) kernel selection policy, (b) KV-cache compatibility layer, (c) fallback and rollback mechanics, and (d) telemetry required to operate safely.
- Surface unresolved engineering risks and propose mitigations and experiments to close them.

Summary of experiments run (high level)
---
1) Baseline: Triton Inference Server (TF/ONNX path) with standard cuBLAS/cuDNN kernels.
2) TensorRT engine from ONNX export, FP16, no dynamic batching (dedicated pool).
3) Custom kernel: fused attention + packed KV layout + int8-weight quantization (our prototype).
4) Hybrid: Triton as broker with TensorRT and custom-kernel backends, switching by model tag.

Key measurements captured: single-request latency (1-token generation after prompt), throughput (tokens/sec with 32 concurrent requests), GPU memory resident (model + kv), KV per-token footprint, percent of requests needing fallback/convert.

Representative numbers (sanity/relative comparisons) — test harness: GPT-like model ~1.3B params, seq len 2048, batch=1 for latency, concurrency sweep for throughput. Numbers are median of 50 runs.
- TensorRT FP16 (dedicated engine): p50 single-token latency ~4.2ms, p95 ~9.1ms; throughput (32 conc) ~210 tokens/s; GPU mem (model+kv warm) ~8.1GB; KV per-token ~0.68KB.
- Triton (onnx runtime + triton optimizations): p50 ~5.9ms, p95 ~12.3ms; throughput ~170 tokens/s; GPU mem ~8.9GB; KV per-token ~0.68KB.
- Custom kernel (fused attention, quantized int8 weights, compressed KV layout): p50 ~3.6ms, p95 ~8.7ms; throughput ~260 tokens/s; GPU mem ~6.2GB; KV per-token ~0.20KB (packed key/value + asymmetric quantization).

Interpretation:
- Custom kernel gives clear advantages in GPU resident size and throughput for our prototype quantization and packed-KV layout at the cost of added complexity (conversion, numerical drift risk).
- TensorRT improves latency relative to Triton/ONNX due to kernel specialization, but doesn't achieve the memory benefits of our custom packed KV/quantization.

KV-cache compatibility issues observed
---
- Layout mismatch: Triton/TensorRT both assume separate KV tensors per layer stored in FP16 contiguous layout. Our custom kernel packs keys/values into fused structures and stores asymmetric quantization parameters per-block. A straightforward pointer swap is impossible.
- Precision mismatch: moving from int8-packed KV to FP16 requires dequantization and expansion, a non-trivial CPU/GPU cost and possible numeric drift.
- Sharding implications: our dedicated-pool autoscaler may move requests between GPUs; a KV format that is backend-specific complicates pre-warming and migration.

Potential approaches to KV compatibility (pros/cons)
---
1) Universal on-the-wire KV format + per-backend adapter
   - Store KV in a canonical serialized layout (e.g., contiguous FP16) in the control plane and convert at the edge to backend-specific layout on first use.
   - Pros: single truth, easy cross-backend migration.
   - Cons: extra conversion cost at first touch; loses memory benefits if persisted as FP16.

2) Backend-native KV with lazy materialization and conversion
   - Persist KV in the format produced by the serving backend. When a request needs to move back to a different backend, convert lazily and cache converted buffers per session.
   - Pros: preserves per-backend memory/throughput benefits; conversions only when necessary.
   - Cons: need multi-format cache entries; risk of cache explosion; added complexity in eviction and accounting.

3) Hybrid policy: allow cross-backend migration only when formats are compatible; otherwise force a cold-start (recompute KV from scratch or replay prompts)
   - Pros: simple; no runtime conversion code paths.
   - Cons: potentially poor UX and higher cost when migrations happen.

Fault-tolerance and fallback strategy
---
- We must avoid silent correctness regressions. My proposal: opt for conservative behavior by default (no automatic cross-format migration) and enable lazy conversion as an opt-in experimental feature with strict telemetry and canary policies.
- Fallbacks for kernel failures:
  - Fast path: if the runtime detects a kernel OOM or kernel launch failure, fallback to a compatible Triton backend for the same model if KV format matches.
  - If KV format is incompatible, trigger one of:
    a) convert KV synchronously (if session is small and customer tolerance is high), or
    b) continue on fallback but mark session as needing cold-replay (enqueue prompt replay and notify caller using an explicit status).

Scheduling and kernel selection policy draft
---
Inputs to selection decision (ranked):
1) model annotation (preferred kernel set specified at model onboarding time)
2) request SLAs / latency budget
3) current GPU utilization and queue depth
4) KV format compatibility with session cache
5) quantization/accuracy constraints (some customers require FP16/FP32 only)

Selection algorithm (sketch):
- Prefer backend annotated by model owner if idle capacity exists.
- If capacity constrained and request is not latency-critical, fall back to high-throughput kernel (custom) or Triton mixed-mode; ensure no format violation.
- When migrating requests between backends, consult KV-cache metadata. If incompatible and customer SLA forbids conversion, return a ‘backend_mismatch’ error and surface resolution paths.

Operational telemetry needed
---
- Per-request metadata: backend chosen, backend version/commit, KV-format-id, conversion performed (Y/N), conversion time, tokens converted, errors.
- Per-session: list of backends used over lifetime, total bytes converted, cold-replay count.
- Alerts: conversion rate spikes, conversion p95 > Xms, fallback frequency by model, cross-backend migration failures.

Safety/Eval harness and tests
---
- Forced conversion tests: replay large sessions through conversion code path; validate numerical drift (BLEU/ROUGE-ish or logprobs) up to acceptable thresholds.
- Stress tests: 1000 concurrent sessions with mixed backends to measure eviction and conversion cascades.
- Accuracy regression: run the same prompts across backends and diff logits/outputs. Flag deltas > threshold.
- End-to-end latency SLO tests with induced kernel OOMs to validate fallback latency and response codes.

Open engineering questions / risks
---
- How expensive is conversion at scale? Need a tight estimate (ms per token) on different GPUs.
- Can we design a compact canonical KV format that preserves memory savings (e.g., block-quantized canonical set)?
- How to charge for conversions in billing? It affects customer expectations.
- Is there a single metadata schema (format-id, quantization-params) that is sufficient for all backends?

Immediate next experiments (actionable)
---
1) Micro-benchmark conversion: implement GPU resident conversion kernels (custom -> FP16, FP16 -> custom) and measure p50/p95 for batches of 1/8/32 tokens. (owners: Daniel, Marco) target week: 2 weeks.
2) Implement KV metadata schema: format-id, quant-params, layer-shape-hash. Use in session store and propagate in tracing. (owner: Lena) target: 1 week.
3) Canary lazy-conversion feature behind flag: enable for internal org traffic only, collect telemetry for 2 weeks, measure conversions/session and latency impact. (owner: Avery + infra) target: 4 weeks.
4) End-to-end accuracy check: run 10k prompts across the three backends and compute distribution of per-token logprob differences. (owner: Sofia) target: 3 weeks.

Low-effort UX mitigations for customers
---
- Model onboarding UI should let owners opt-in to backend pool (e.g., enable custom-kernel if they allow quantization).
- Expose an explicit session-level flag to allow conversion or reject migrations.
- Return clear error codes when a session cannot be migrated due to format mismatch (so clients can retry or replay).

Notes to reviewers
---
- This document is intentionally exploratory; numbers are preliminary and environment-specific. The goal is to capture the tradeoffs and a pragmatic rollout plan. Please add feedback inline or on the linked PR/Jira.

Action items (short)
---
- Approve micro-benchmark effort and allocate 1 GPU/week for conversion kernels.
- Add KV-format metadata to session store schema (small change).
- Agreement on conservative default: do not auto-convert cross-backend unless feature-flagged.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Daniel for the initial prototype kernels, Marco for setting up the Triton+TensorRT cluster, and Sofia for running the accuracy harness.
